stage.title: Three books meet a living world
stage.motivation: Fleet prey dominates a food shortage. Follow an invented wolf dossier from 10 faster + 10 slower parents to 15 faster + 5 slower recruits. What do inheritance, population pressure and deep time explain—and what does one count leave open?

objectives.text: Explain the 50% → 75% change and its limits

reading.text: Darwin drew on Lyell’s geological work while reaching conclusions Lyell did not initially share. A book can make a new argument possible without its author agreeing with the result.
reading.attribution: Historical paraphrase; University of Edinburgh and Darwin Correspondence Project accounts.

reading.text: One invented local wolf population starts with 10 faster and 10 slower breeding adults, classified by running records, not appearance. Fleet prey dominates during a food shortage. Both groups retain the other abilities needed to live and catch prey. Speed is advantageous only under the specified conditions, not a universal ranking.
reading.attribution: Authored, invented one-generation teaching dossier, adapted from Darwin’s explicitly imaginary wolf/prey example (Origin, 1859, IV, pp.90–91); not historical measurements or a realistic wolf population model.

reading.text: For this toy generation, F1–F5 are five pairs of faster adults; S1–S5 are five pairs of slower adults. Each pair has four pups. Stipulate that offspring retain their parents’ speed category because the difference is inherited, not learned through rearing. Only same-category pairs are included. This supplied premise is not inferred from photographs or from resemblance alone; it does not explain the physical mechanism of inheritance.
reading.attribution: Authored, invented one-generation teaching dossier, adapted from Darwin’s explicitly imaginary wolf/prey example (Origin, 1859, IV, pp.90–91); not historical measurements or a realistic wolf population model.

reading.text: Invented recruitment ledger: each of F1–F5 produces 4 faster pups, of whom 3 reach the next breeding cohort: 20 born, 15 recruited. Each of S1–S5 produces 4 slower pups, of whom 1 recruits: 20 born, 5 recruited. Each pup is counted once under its parental pair. In this stipulated case, speed improves obtaining scarce fleet prey and hence recruitment. The other 20 pups do not breed in this cohort; births alone are not reproductive success.
reading.attribution: Authored, invented one-generation teaching dossier, adapted from Darwin’s explicitly imaginary wolf/prey example (Origin, 1859, IV, pp.90–91); not historical measurements or a realistic wolf population model.

reading.text: The first breeding cohort has 10 faster + 10 slower adults = 20. Its 40 offspring supply a separate next breeding cohort: 15 faster + 5 slower = 20. No original adults are included in that second count, and no migrants enter it. Compare the two cohorts, not 20 parents plus 20 recruits. This is one invented transition, not a measured time series or a forecast of later generations.
reading.attribution: Authored, invented one-generation teaching dossier, adapted from Darwin’s explicitly imaginary wolf/prey example (Origin, 1859, IV, pp.90–91); not historical measurements or a realistic wolf population model.

reading.text: One argument said that domestic varieties tending to revert showed natural varieties must remain within fixed bounds. Wallace’s 1858 essay challenged that inference: conditions outside domestication differ, and a variety can persist or depart further when it fits those conditions. He developed his reasoning independently; it was presented with Darwin’s work in 1858. This is a substantive contrasting argument, not just a second signature.
reading.attribution: Historical paraphrase of Wallace’s 1858 essay, pp.53–54, 60–62, and the joint publication’s introductory letter; no quotation. The numerical wolf dossier is our invention.

reading.text: The earlier geological record supplied a sequence of processes, not a biological cause. Long time allows successive inherited changes to accumulate if conditions and reproduction keep favoring them; time alone selects nothing. It cannot turn our one-generation count into a record of an entire species’ past. Lyell’s influence did not mean agreement with every evolutionary conclusion.
reading.attribution: Authored connection to the earlier geological investigation; historical context from Darwin, Origin (1859), IV, pp.95–96, and the existing Lyell dossier.

reading.text: The archive preserves the identities and running records of the 10 faster and 10 slower adults. The first cohort is therefore half faster. Images can identify specimens, but a still photograph alone measures neither running speed nor inheritance. The archive is a teaching documentation method, not a reconstruction of Darwin’s exact workflow.
reading.attribution: Authored, invented one-generation teaching dossier, adapted from Darwin’s explicitly imaginary wolf/prey example (Origin, 1859, IV, pp.90–91); not historical measurements or a realistic wolf population model.

reading.text: The running dossier supplies an existing difference; the separate inheritance premise says the 20 pups of faster pairs are faster and the 20 pups of slower pairs are slower. Together these provide transmissible variation for this model. A catalogue of appearances would not supply that premise. No individual needs to acquire extra speed during its own lifetime for this particular population change.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.

reading.text: The population pamphlet’s growth constraint becomes a biological question: which offspring join the next breeding cohort? Here 40 pups are born but only 20 recruit under the stated food shortage. Excess offspring supplies a constraint, not an explanation of which trait increases. The ledger must also connect the inherited difference to unequal recruitment. This is not a rule for human institutions.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.

reading.text: Birth output is equal: 4 pups per pair in both groups. Recruitment differs: each faster pair contributes 3 next-generation breeders, each slower pair 1. Across five pairs each, that is 15 faster recruits versus 5 slower. Each recruit is counted once, not once for each parent. The model supplies a speed-related feeding advantage under fleet-prey scarcity; a small count alone would not establish that cause.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.

reading.text: Initial faster share: 10/(10+10) = 10/20 = 50%. Next-cohort faster share: 15/(15+5) = 15/20 = 75%. That is a rise of 25 percentage points, while the cohort total stays 20. The slower share falls from 50% to 25%. The population’s composition changes; the parents do not turn into their faster offspring.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.

reading.text: The 50% → 75% shift follows from existing faster/slower variation, stipulated transmission, and the supplied difference in breeding recruitment under fleet-prey scarcity. More births alone and more time alone are insufficient. Repetition could accumulate change, but these conditions need not persist: neither endless increase in speed nor inevitable progress follows. This one-generation model does not reconstruct the history of all species.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.

reading.text: Our supplied 50% → 75% change does not show whether later generations would return to the starting mixture. Wallace’s argument challenges a supposed compulsory return of natural varieties to an original type; Darwin’s imagined predator case asks how existing differences can be favored under changed prey conditions. These are related, independent lines of reasoning, not identical experiments. Our one transition does not establish indefinite divergence.
reading.attribution: Authored comparison of the invented dossier with Darwin, Origin (1859), IV, pp.90–91, and Wallace’s 1858 essay, pp.53–54, 60–62; no quotation.

items.label: Model works; count alone does not prove cause

reading.text: Reuse the water investigation’s discipline: separate the recorded contrast from the causal claim. The invented cohort count establishes 50% → 75%; selection follows here because inheritance and speed-related recruitment were supplied as premises. A single small real-world count would not by itself distinguish selection from random sampling (drift), migration, or measurement error. A real investigation needs independent inheritance evidence, recruitment tracking, repeated comparisons and tests of alternatives.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.

reading.text: The checked edition keeps the ledger and its limits together: 10 faster + 10 slower parents; 40 pups; 15 faster + 5 slower next breeders. Inherited differences and unequal recruitment under the specified conditions explain this model’s change. Population pressure poses the constraint; deep time permits repetition; evidence discipline prevents overclaiming. This invented example neither proves every species’ history nor supplies a moral or policy rule for human society.
reading.attribution: Authored inference from the stipulated teaching dossier; not a historical quotation or a statistical finding from wild wolves.
